questions.text: What is the argument order for grep?
options: It depends on whether the pattern is a regular expression
grep PATTERN FILE — the pattern first, then the files to search
questions.explanation: Everything after the first non-option argument is treated as a file to search. With no file at all, grep reads standard input — which is what makes … | grep pattern work.

questions.text: Why is the pattern in grep 'disk full' app.log quoted?
options: So the shell passes it to grep as one argument, and does not touch its special characters
So grep treats it as a regular expression rather than a fixed string
questions.explanation: Without quotes the space would split it into two arguments, and characters like * or $ could be eaten or expanded by the shell before grep ever sees them. Single quotes are the safe default.

questions.text: What does grep -c ERROR app.log print for this file?
questions.context:
$ cat app.log
2024-01-05 INFO  user devasc logged in
2024-01-05 ERROR disk full on /dev/sda1
2024-01-06 WARN  retry 3 of 5
2024-01-06 error lowercase spelling
2024-01-07 INFO  cpu 85% load
2024-01-07 ERROR timeout after 30s
questions.explanation: Verified by running it. Only the two uppercase ERROR lines match — the lowercase error line does not, because grep is case-sensitive by default.

questions.text: And grep -ic error app.log?
questions.context:
$ cat app.log
2024-01-05 INFO  user devasc logged in
2024-01-05 ERROR disk full on /dev/sda1
2024-01-06 WARN  retry 3 of 5
2024-01-06 error lowercase spelling
2024-01-07 INFO  cpu 85% load
2024-01-07 ERROR timeout after 30s
questions.explanation: Verified: -i ignores case, so the two ERROR lines and the lowercase error line all count.

questions.text: What does grep -vc INFO app.log print?
questions.context:
$ cat app.log
2024-01-05 INFO  user devasc logged in
2024-01-05 ERROR disk full on /dev/sda1
2024-01-06 WARN  retry 3 of 5
2024-01-06 error lowercase spelling
2024-01-07 INFO  cpu 85% load
2024-01-07 ERROR timeout after 30s
questions.explanation: Verified. -v inverts the match, so it counts the lines without INFO: 6 lines total minus the 2 INFO lines.

questions.text: What does grep -n WARN app.log print?
questions.context:
$ cat app.log
2024-01-05 INFO  user devasc logged in
2024-01-05 ERROR disk full on /dev/sda1
2024-01-06 WARN  retry 3 of 5
2024-01-06 error lowercase spelling
2024-01-07 INFO  cpu 85% load
2024-01-07 ERROR timeout after 30s
questions.explanation: Verified. -n prefixes each matching line with its line number in the file, separated by a colon.

questions.text: What is the difference between grep -c and grep -o pattern file | wc -l?
options: -c counts matching lines; the second counts every match, including several on one line
-o only works on one file at a time
-c counts matches and the second counts lines
questions.explanation: Verified on a line reading aaa bbb aaa: grep -c aaa printed 1 while grep -o aaa | wc -l printed 2. This trips people up when counting occurrences rather than lines.

questions.text: Match each grep option to what it does.
allChoices: Inverts the match — prints the lines that do not match
Prefixes each result with its line number
Prints only the count of matching lines
Prints only the names of the files that contain a match
Prints only the matched part of the line, not the whole line

pairs.match: Inverts the match — prints the lines that do not match
Prefixes each result with its line number
Prints only the count of matching lines
Prints only the names of the files that contain a match
Prints only the matched part of the line, not the whole line

questions.explanation: The six you will reach for most often. Verified each against a sample file.

questions.text: What does grep -l ERROR *.log give you, and what does -L give instead?
options: They both list matching files, but -L uses full paths
-l lists the files that contain a match; -L lists the files that do not
-l lists matching lines; -L lists long lines
questions.explanation: Verified: with app.log containing ERROR and users.txt not, -l printed app.log and -L printed users.txt. -l stops reading each file at the first hit, so it is fast on large trees.

questions.text: Which lines does grep -w bin users.txt match?
options: No lines, because no field is exactly bin
The three lines with /bin/bash or /bin/false — the slashes make bin a whole word there
Only the daemon and sshd lines, because of /usr/sbin
questions.explanation: Verified: 3 lines (root, devasc, mysql). -w requires the match to be bounded by non-word characters, and / qualifies — but sbin does not, because s is a word character.

questions.text: What does -x require, as in grep -x root users.txt?
options: That the file be searched backwards
That the pattern match a whole word
That the pattern match the whole line, start to finish
questions.explanation: Verified on a file containing root and rootkit: grep -cx root returned 1. -w is the word-level version of the same idea.

questions.text: What does grep -r 'TODO' . do?
options: Reverses the sense of the match
Searches only the current directory, ignoring subdirectories
Searches every file under the current directory, recursively
questions.explanation: Verified. Results come back as path:line. -r follows no symlinks; -R does.

questions.text: Why would you use grep -q pattern file inside a script?
options: It prints nothing and just sets the exit status, which the script can test
It makes the search quicker by reading only the first line
It queues the search to run in the background
questions.explanation: Quiet mode. It also exits as soon as it finds the first match. Pair it with if grep -q …; then.

questions.text: What are grep's three exit statuses?
options: 0 = something matched, 1 = nothing matched, 2 = an error such as a missing file
0 = nothing matched, 1 = something matched, 2 = an error
It always returns 0 unless the pattern is invalid
questions.explanation: Verified all three by running them. Note that “no match” being a non-zero status will stop a script running under set -e.

questions.text: What do -A 2, -B 2 and -C 2 add to the output?
options: 2 lines before, 2 after, and 2 in colour
The 2nd match only, in three different formats
2 lines after the match, 2 before it, and 2 on each side
questions.explanation: Verified with -A1 on a log. After (A), before (B), context on both sides (C) — indispensable for reading stack traces out of a log.

questions.text: What is grep -e ERROR -e WARN app.log for?
options: Reading the patterns from a file
Searching for more than one pattern in a single pass
Escaping the patterns so they are treated literally
questions.explanation: Verified. -e can be repeated; -f patterns.txt reads a whole list from a file; and in ERE the same thing can be written grep -E 'ERROR|WARN'.

questions.text: What does -F do, as in grep -F 'a.c' file?
options: Treats the pattern as a fixed string, so . means a literal dot
Forces the search to keep going after an error
Matches only at the start of the line
Reads the pattern from a file
questions.explanation: Verified: on a file containing a.c and abc, grep -F 'a.c' matched only a.c, while plain grep 'a.c' matched both. -F is also what the old fgrep did.

questions.text: Which options change whether grep prints the filename alongside each match? (Select three answers)
options: -l — show only the filename, not the line
questions.explanation: Verified -H and -h on a single file. By default grep prints filenames only when searching more than one file, which is exactly when a script parsing the output gets surprised — force it either way with -H or -h.

questions.text: What does grep -c '^d' users.txt return?
questions.explanation: Verified: the daemon and devasc lines. ^ anchors the match to the start of the line.

questions.text: What does grep -c 'bash$' users.txt return?
questions.explanation: Verified: root and devasc, the two accounts whose line ends in /bin/bash. $ anchors to the end of the line.

questions.text: What does the pattern '^$' match?
options: Lines containing a literal dollar sign
Empty lines — start of line immediately followed by end of line
questions.explanation: Verified: grep -c '^$' on a file with three blank lines returned 3. grep -v '^$' file is the usual way to strip blank lines out of a config.

questions.text: In a regular expression, what does . match?
options: Exactly one character, whatever it is
questions.explanation: Verified: grep 'a.c' matched both abc and a.c. To mean a literal dot, escape it: grep 'a\.c' matched only a.c.

questions.text: Fill in what makes this pattern match a literal dot, so it finds the file name and not abc as well.
questions.explanation: A backslash escapes the metacharacter that follows it. Verified: grep -c 'a\.c' returned 1 where the unescaped version returned 2.

questions.text: What does * mean in a regular expression?
options: Zero or more of the item immediately before it
Any run of characters, as in a filename wildcard
questions.explanation: This is the classic confusion: in the shell, *.log means any filename ending in .log, but in a regex * repeats what precedes it. The regex for “anything” is .*.

questions.text: In a basic regular expression (plain grep), what does grep 'a+' file match?
options: Lines containing one or more a characters
questions.explanation: Verified against a file containing a, aa and a+: it matched only a+. In BRE, + and ? are ordinary characters — write a\+, or switch to grep -E.

questions.text: Which two are equivalent?
questions.explanation: Verified: both returned the same three lines. -E switches to extended regular expressions, where + ? { } ( ) | are metacharacters without backslashes — this is what egrep used to be.

questions.text: How do you write “this pattern or that one” in plain grep, without -E?
questions.explanation: Verified: grep -c 'root\|daemon' and grep -cE 'root|daemon' both returned 2. The escaped form is a GNU extension — the -E version is the portable one.

questions.text: What does grep -cE 'nologin|false' users.txt return?
questions.explanation: Verified: daemon and sshd end in nologin, mysql ends in /bin/false — the three accounts that cannot log in interactively.

questions.text: What does {2,4} mean in an extended regular expression?
options: Between 2 and 4 repetitions of the preceding item
Between 2 and 4 characters of any kind
questions.explanation: Verified: grep -cE 'a{3}' matched aaa and aaaa but not aa. {3} is exactly three, {3,} is three or more.

questions.text: What does grep -cE '[0-9]{3}' users.txt return?
questions.explanation: Verified: devasc (900), mysql (113/120) and sshd (112/65534). The root and daemon lines only have single-digit ids.

questions.text: What is the difference between [0-9] and [^0-9]?
options: The second matches any single character that is not a digit
The second matches a literal caret followed by a digit
The second anchors the digit to the start of the line
Nothing — the caret is ignored inside brackets
questions.explanation: A caret means “negated” only as the first character inside the brackets; anywhere else it is a literal caret. Verified: grep -cE '^[^r]' on the 5-line users file returned 4 — every line except root's.

questions.text: What is [[:digit:]]?
options: A backreference to an earlier group
A literal match for the text [:digit:]
A POSIX character class, equivalent to [0-9]
A Perl-only shorthand that grep does not support
questions.explanation: The POSIX classes — [[:digit:]], [[:alpha:]], [[:alnum:]], [[:space:]], [[:upper:]] — are locale-aware, so they keep working with accented letters where [a-z] quietly does not. Note the double brackets: the class goes inside a bracket expression.

questions.text: What do \< and \> do in grep '\<cat\>' file?
options: Match a literal less-than and greater-than sign
Anchor the match to a word boundary, so catalog does not match
Mark the start and end of a group
questions.explanation: Verified on cat / catalog / “the cat sat”: it matched 2 lines, skipping catalog. grep -w cat is the readable shorthand for the same thing.

questions.text: What does the pattern -E '(..)\1' find?
options: Any two characters immediately repeated, such as abab
Two groups separated by a backslash
Exactly four characters of any kind
questions.explanation: Verified: it matched abab and xyxy but not abcd. \1 is a backreference to whatever the first parenthesised group captured — not the pattern, the actual text it matched.

questions.text: Which flag turns on Perl-compatible regular expressions, giving you \d, \w and lookarounds?
questions.explanation: -P is a GNU grep feature and is not available everywhere (it is also refused in some locales), so scripts that need to be portable stick to -E.

questions.text: Fill in the flag that finds every line mentioning timeout, whatever the capitalisation.
questions.explanation: Case-insensitive matching. Without it, Timeout and TIMEOUT are missed.

questions.text: Fill in the flag that shows every line except the ones mentioning INFO.
questions.explanation: Invert the match. Chaining them — grep -v INFO app.log | grep -v WARN — is a common way to whittle a log down to what is actually wrong.

questions.text: Fill in the two anchors so this matches only lines that consist of nothing else — blank lines — and delete them from the config.
questions.explanation: Start immediately followed by end. Verified: on a file with three blank lines grep -c '^$' returned 3.

questions.text: Fill in the option that makes grep search every file under the current directory.
questions.explanation: Recursive. Well worth pairing with -n so you get the line numbers too.

questions.text: Fill in the flag that switches grep to extended regular expressions, so the pipe means alternation.
questions.explanation: Without -E the pipe is just a literal character and the pattern matches nothing. Verified both forms against the log.

questions.text: Why does ps -ef | grep sshd usually show one more line than you expect?
options: ps prints each process once per thread
The grep sshd process is itself running, and matches its own pattern
questions.explanation: The classic. Fixes: ps -ef | grep -v grep | grep sshd, the trick pattern grep '[s]shd', or just use pgrep sshd.

questions.text: What is grep reading in dmesg | grep -i usb?
options: Nothing; this is a syntax error
Standard input — the output of the command before the pipe
questions.explanation: With no filename, grep reads stdin. This is what makes it the universal filter — it can sit at the end of any pipeline.

questions.text: Which command finds the .conf files containing listen 80, searching only .conf files?
questions.explanation: --include filters which files a recursive search opens. The third option is a trap: piping find into grep searches the file names, not the contents — for that you want find /etc -name '*.conf' -exec grep -l 'listen 80' {} +.

questions.text: grep 'Error' and grep 'error' return the same lines unless you add -i.
questions.explanation: False — that is precisely the point of -i. Verified on the log: grep -c ERROR returned 2 and grep -ic error returned 3.

questions.text: Match each companion tool to the job it does in a pipeline.
allChoices: Slices a chosen field out of each line, by delimiter
Puts the lines in order, which uniq depends on
Collapses adjacent duplicate lines and counts them
Counts how many lines came through
Translates one set of characters into another
Substitutes text as the lines stream past

pairs.match: Slices a chosen field out of each line, by delimiter
Puts the lines in order, which uniq depends on
Collapses adjacent duplicate lines and counts them
Counts how many lines came through
Translates one set of characters into another
Substitutes text as the lines stream past

questions.explanation: grep decides which lines; these decide what happens to them. Every one of these was verified by running it.

questions.text: What does cut -d: -f1 users.txt print?
options: The five login shells, one per line
The first line of the file
The five usernames, one per line
The whole file, with colons removed
questions.explanation: Verified: root, daemon, devasc, mysql, sshd. -f1,7 would give the username and the shell.

questions.text: What does echo 'a a a' | sed 's/a/b/' print, and how do you change all three?
options: b b b — it is global by default
a a a — sed needs -i to change anything
questions.explanation: Verified both. s/// replaces the first match on each line; s///g replaces every match on the line. -i is a separate thing again — it edits the file in place instead of printing.

questions.text: What does awk -F: '$3 >= 900 {print $1}' users.txt print?
questions.explanation: Verified. -F: splits on colons, $3 is the UID and $1 the username — only devasc's UID of 900 passes the test. This is the standard way to list real user accounts as opposed to service ones.

questions.text: Why is sort access.log | uniq -c | sort -nr | head the standard “top offenders” pipeline?
options: uniq needs its duplicates adjacent, so you sort first, count, then sort numerically by that count
sort must run twice because it is unstable
questions.explanation: Verified the uniq half: unsorted input gave six groups of 1, sorted input gave apple 3, banana 2, cherry 1. sort -nr then puts the biggest count on top.

questions.text: Which of these produce a count of ERROR lines in app.log? (Select three answers)
questions.explanation: All three return 2 on this file (verified). -o prints the matched text without counting, -n numbers the lines it prints, and the sed command edits the text rather than counting anything.
